approachQuestion.prompt: An expression contains leaves and binary JOIN operations. Either child may be evaluated first. Each leaf evaluation produces one stored result. A JOIN needs both child results simultaneously and replaces them with one result in place, using no extra result slot. No child may be recomputed or saved outside these slots. Return the smallest possible peak number of result slots needed to evaluate the root. Examples: a leaf needs 1; JOIN(leaf,leaf) needs 2; JOIN(JOIN(leaf,leaf),leaf) needs 2.
constraints: The read-only expression is a finite unshared binary tree with n nodes, 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000, and height h ≤ 1000.
An operator must completely evaluate one child before starting the other. Leaf payloads and operator results are irrelevant to the required slot count.
Return the slot count only; the solver is not actually evaluating or storing the expression results. Integer arithmetic takes constant time.

options.text: Always evaluate the smaller-requirement child first and use max(smaller,1+larger).
options.feedback: For child requirements 2 and 1, this predicts 3; evaluating the requirement-2 child first achieves 2.

options.text: Return 1 for a leaf. Obtain child requirements a and b; if a=b return a+1, otherwise return max(a,b), corresponding to evaluating the larger-requirement child first.
options.feedback: The first result occupies one slot during the second child; unequal requirements absorb that held result when the larger child is done first.

options.text: Enumerate every possible child-order assignment, simulate its slot usage, and take the minimum.
options.feedback: It explores an enormous number of orderings even though two child summaries determine the optimum locally.
JOIN(JOIN(leaf,leaf),leaf) needs 2 slots, not 3, because completed child temporaries can be reused.

feedback.reason: If child requirements differ, evaluate the larger-requirement child first; its saved result still fits while evaluating the smaller.
details: Recursively return the minimal slot requirement of a subtree. A leaf returns 1. For a JOIN, compute both requirements; equal requirements r return r+1, and unequal requirements return their maximum. This computes a number without actually evaluating the represented expression.

If child requirements differ, evaluate the larger-requirement child first; its saved result still fits while evaluating the smaller. Equal requirements need one extra slot. The computed slot count is output data, not the solver's own frame usage.
“Always evaluate the smaller-requirement child first and use max(smaller,1+larger).”: For child requirements 2 and 1, this predicts 3; evaluating the requirement-2 child first achieves 2.

“Return 1 for a leaf. Obtain child requirements a and b; if a=b return a+1, otherwise return max(a,b), corresponding to evaluating the larger-requirement child first.”: The first result occupies one slot during the second child; unequal requirements absorb that held result when the larger child is done first.

“Enumerate every possible child-order assignment, simulate its slot usage, and take the minimum.”: It explores an enormous number of orderings even though two child summaries determine the optimum locally.
“Return a+b for every JOIN.”: JOIN(JOIN(leaf,leaf),leaf) needs 2 slots, not 3, because completed child temporaries can be reused.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let n and h have the meanings in Q1. Use child indices and references without copying lists. Count active call frames; exclude input and returned output. There is no tail-call elimination. No hashing is used. Here n is expression node count and h is expression height; distinguish the hypothetical result slots being computed from the solver's own storage. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Compute one slot summary per node using a depth-sized recursion stack.
details: The solver computes one constant-sized summary per node, each once. It retains only recursive frames along a root-to-leaf path; its space is not the slot count returned as data.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Nested calls remain active along a path; their storage must be counted.
“O(n²) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: Each object is processed once without rescanning or copying its descendants.
“O(h + 1) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: A shallow but wide input can still require inspecting every object.
